title: Ministers respond: limited neuroscience evidence, precautionary measures and a patchwork of policies for children online
label: 3 November 2026 · Neuroscience and digital childhoods
summary: Ministers and officials from DCMS, DHSC and DfE told the Committee that long-term causal evidence linking children’s brain development to screen use is limited, so government is funding research, issuing precautionary guidance (especially for under-fives), and introducing a package of online-safety measures (including an under-16 social media ban, feature restrictions and researcher access to platform data). They disagreed about how definitive the evidence is, stressed the harms are broader than 'screen time' (content, contact and features matter), and discussed the need for better data from platforms, safety-by-design for products, and support for alternatives like sport and youth services.

chapters.title: What evidence do we have — and what’s missing
chapters.takeaway: Ministers say the causal neuroscience evidence linking screens to brain development is limited; government is funding research and using expert groups to guide precautionary policy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This is the final session in our inquiry; we want to know how Government uses evidence on digital tech and children’s development. Please introduce yourselves when you answer.

turns.speaker: Tabitha Jay
turns.text: I’m Tabitha Jay from DHSC. We work with expert advisory groups on guidance for 0–5s and are looking at 5–18s. We know the evidence is partial and the NIHR is investing money in this area.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: I’m Minister for Public Health. Evidence is limited; longitudinal studies help but technology evolves fast. We must act where there’s a credible risk—hence 0–5 guidance—and we’re working across departments.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okubo
turns.text: I’m from DCMS. Tech moves fast, so we need early-warning signals. The independent regulator Ofcom runs user surveys and we’ve commissioned academic reviews showing many studies are low quality but associations with harm exist.

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: I’m Minister at DCMS. Parents want help now. Beyond neuroscience we look at a spectrum of harms: content, contact and physical harms like poor sleep. We’ll regulate platforms and give researchers access to platform data.

turns.speaker: Paul Waugh
turns.text: I’m Minister for Early Education. The causal evidence is thin, but correlations with delays and attention exist. We used a precautionary principle for 0–5 guidance and are reviewing education and physical displacement effects.

turns.speaker: Michael Thomas
turns.text: I’m DfE’s Chief Scientific Adviser. We have many ongoing studies, including randomized trials (e.g. delaying smartphone issuance), longitudinal cohorts, and work on AI’s effects on learning, but research can lag behind tech change.

chapters.title: Precautionary guidance for very young children
chapters.takeaway: Government used a precautionary approach for under-fives, focusing on reduced screen time, joint media use, and protecting early attachment.

turns.speaker: Emily Darlington
turns.text: What was the evidence for the 0–5 guidance, and will you publish guidance for older children?

turns.speaker: Paul Waugh
turns.text: 0–5 guidance used strong correlations—language, attention and sociability links—and was co-produced with teachers and parents. We will publish 5–18 guidance in the coming months or early next year.

turns.speaker: Kit Malthouse
turns.text: Do you all accept that screens change brain development in young children?

turns.speaker: Paul Waugh
turns.text: Screens influence development, but we must distinguish correlation from causation. That’s why we want better causal evidence.

turns.speaker: Michael Thomas
turns.text: Brain development is experience-dependent, so screen experiences will shape it—but detailed causal links are not well established yet.

turns.speaker: Tabitha Jay
turns.text: Attachment, facial contact and parent–child interaction were considered in the guidance. The guidance emphasises being present and avoiding fast-paced screen content for under-twos.

turns.speaker: Kit Malthouse
turns.text: Is there research on 'technoference'—parents’ screen use affecting infant attachment?

turns.speaker: Tabitha Jay
turns.text: Parental attachment research informed the guidance; I can follow up on specific technoference studies.

chapters.title: Policy actions while evidence is assembled
chapters.takeaway: Ministers stress they are acting now—under-16 social media ban, feature restrictions, and steps on chatbots—while also commissioning research and briefing Ofcom to monitor effects.

turns.speaker: Emily Darlington
turns.text: What role should platforms play in producing safety research when they launch products?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: Under the Online Safety Act, platforms must assess and mitigate risks. We will allow verified researchers access to platform data so academics can study harms properly.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okubo
turns.text: Ofcom will require transparency reports; we’ll consult on the exact researcher-data access regime and the data fields researchers need.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What data will researchers get? For example, counts of underage users, sharing patterns, or algorithm weights?

turns.speaker: Daniel Okubo
turns.text: We’ll consult on that by the end of the year. We must balance useful research data with privacy; transparency reports already coming next year will publish more platform information.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Has Ofcom used its powers to inspect algorithms or issued transparency notices yet?

turns.speaker: Daniel Okubo
turns.text: I’ll confirm in writing; the transparency reporting powers for category 1 services come into effect next year and Ofcom has request powers now.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will the UK expect platforms to bring to the UK the protections they agreed in the US Meta settlement?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: If measures reduce harm they should be implemented here. We are going further in places—under-16 ban and feature limits—so we’re considering what read-across makes sense. I’ll supply analysis to the Committee.

chapters.title: Age cut-offs, functionality and design
chapters.takeaway: Age thresholds are a policy judgment; ministers will regulate by the harmful features and functions of services rather than by label alone, with Ofcom deciding scope against criteria.

turns.speaker: Martin Wrigley
turns.text: Why 16 for the social media ban? Brain development continues past 16—how did you pick the age?

turns.speaker: Daniel Okubo
turns.text: There’s no hard causal evidence to pick an exact age. The Online Safety Act already protects under-18s from certain content. The 16 limit is a policy judgment informed by consultation, behavioural issues and practicality.

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: We wanted to avoid a cliff edge at 16 and to protect younger adolescents who are most affected by attention-grabbing features. It’s a policy, not a neuroscientific bright line.

turns.speaker: Martin Wrigley
turns.text: Will restrictions be defined by features and functions rather than by calling a service 'social media'?

turns.speaker: Daniel Okubo
turns.text: Yes—scope will be criteria-based. Ofcom will assess services against those criteria, so a publisher cannot avoid regulation by using a different label.

turns.speaker: Tom Collins
turns.text: Is the Government pushing a 'safety by design' test so products must not target attention or exploit vulnerabilities?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: We want safe-by-design platforms. Many harmful features—autoplay, infinite scroll, personalised feeds—are under scrutiny. If a product can be designed to be safe it should be.

chapters.title: Sleep, displacement, youth services and edtech safety
chapters.takeaway: Ministers link screen time to sleep and physical inactivity, are funding school and youth alternatives, and are developing safety standards and trials for edtech and AI in education.

turns.speaker: Freddie van Mierlo
turns.text: One in five kids stay up late on TikTok. What tools will the Government use to limit late-night use?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: Measures include parental controls, curfews, default settings, and removing harmful features. We are considering many options and want to limit the time young people spend online late at night.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: We know social media use harms sleep—later bedtimes, shorter sleep—so guidance limits screen time before bed. For young children we recommend 10–14 hours’ sleep and max one hour screen for 2–5s with an adult.

turns.speaker: Paul Waugh
turns.text: Displacement matters: time on screens replaces exercise and social interaction. We’re funding breakfast clubs, enrichment, sports and youth services to give children attractive off-screen activities.

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: DCMS’s youth strategy and funding aim to provide 'somewhere to go, something to do, someone who cares'—we’re investing in youth workers and community programmes alongside the bans.

turns.speaker: Samantha Niblett
turns.text: How will you ensure edtech helps learning rather than purely increasing screen time?

turns.speaker: Paul Waugh
turns.text: DfE is running trials, certifications and co-production with teachers. We’re testing AI tutoring tools, developing safety standards and a certification regime so schools know what is safe and effective.

turns.speaker: Michael Thomas
turns.text: We’re doing randomized trials, rapid evaluations and long-term research to identify which edtech benefits learning and when it harms it.

turns.speaker: Emily Darlington
turns.text: What about unregulated 'homework' chatbots that can groom or isolate children?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: We’re addressing chatbots: some illegal content duties will come under the Crime and Policing Act and we plan future regulation on harmful but legal chatbot harms; they may be in scope.

turns.speaker: Tom Collins
turns.text: Some experts say LLMs may be unsuitable for under-18s because of attachment and social-norm risks. Will you consider a blanket restriction?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: We’re aware of those concerns and will consider harms across the spectrum; legislation and the Online Safety Act duties are part of the approach, but we’re still working out scope for newer AI features.

chapters.title: Data, research and accountability
chapters.takeaway: Ministers acknowledged a data gap: they will consult on verified researcher access to platform data, Ofcom transparency reporting, and committed to follow-up research and evaluations of the ban.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Platforms hold vast data—why hasn’t government used it to study harms earlier?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: That’s the gap we’re trying to plug. We will consult on what platform data researchers need, and Ofcom will require transparency reports once the next tranche of duties starts.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okubo
turns.text: We’ll consult by the end of the year on researcher access. Ofcom will publish transparency reports for category 1 services next year and can already request information from platforms.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will you write to us with details: how many transparency notices Ofcom has issued, the read-across from the US Meta cases, and the list of ongoing trials?

turns.speaker: Daniel Okubo
turns.text: Yes—we will write on transparency notices and the specifics of Ofcom powers.

turns.speaker: Michael Thomas
turns.text: There are ongoing randomized trials—delaying smartphones, restricting social media exposure—and we can share those trial details for scientific scrutiny.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Finally, can you promise to keep building the evidence base to justify the under-16 ban and report outcomes?

turns.speaker: Ian Murray
turns.text: We took the decision to act now. We’ll analyse impacts—Ofcom, academic studies and international comparisons will produce evidence. I’ll supply the Committee further analysis.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. We expect the promised follow-up material and clarity on data, Ofcom notices, and which US measures we want mirrored here.
